title: What to Know About Meta’s Muse AI Security and Privacy Risks
snippet: Meta's Muse AI agent builds a profile on users instantly, raising serious questions about data privacy and agentic AI security standards.
bullets: Meta's Muse AI agent can quietly build a profile on you the second you start using it [1].
An AppleInsider report showed Muse synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user's Apple Messages without consent [1].
Surfshark found that Meta Muse attempts to collect 31 out of 35 types of data, including sensitive personal information [1].

report.t: Meta's Muse AI has been shown to harvest private messages and data even when full disk access is turned off [1]. It collects sensitive personal information like location data and sexual orientation at higher rates than competing chatbots [1].

Security researchers demonstrated the assistant could be hijacked via an easy zero-day exploit [1]. In another instance, Muse mistakenly shared a tech reviewer's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace [1].

Meta feeds conversations into its AI training pipeline by default, leaving it up to users to manually opt out in settings [1]. The tool also asks for access to passwords, emails, calendar invites, and WhatsApp chats [1].

why: Understanding agentic AI privacy risks helps you protect your business communications, personal messages, and sensitive data when adopting new automation tools.
tryit: Check your current AI app permissions and settings to ensure you have manually opted out of data training pipelines and restricted disk access.
qa: What data does Meta Muse collect?
It attempts to collect 31 out of 35 types of data, including location data, sexual orientation, genetic information, and biometric data [1].
Can Muse access data without permission?
Yes, reports showed Muse synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user's Apple Messages even when full disk access was turned off [1].
Does Meta use conversations for training?
Yes, Meta feeds your conversations into its AI training pipeline by default until you manually opt out in the settings [1].
What happened on Facebook Marketplace?
Muse mistakenly shared a Toronto tech reviewer's home address with a potential buyer without his explicit consent [1].

sources.title: What to Learn About Meta’s Muse AI Before It Learns Too Much About You - CNET

title: Build a thriving side hustle by starting small and beating overwhelm

title: How Gray Box Stages and AI Are Speeding Up Filmmaking

report.t: Filming in a gray box with neutral-colored walls offers more flexible shots than traditional green screens [1]. Bright green or blue hues can reflect onto objects and skin, whereas gray boxes avoid this issue [1].

Combining gray boxes with AI-assisted backgrounds speeds up post-production significantly [1]. Dave Clark notes that crews save hours because they do not have to waste time changing lighting or physical setups [1].

Most environments are built by human 3D renderers and visual effects artists using AI as a supporting tool [1]. Disney executives emphasize that technology exists to support creators rather than replace human storytelling [1].

title: How Simple Moss Can Cool Urban Heatwaves and Transform City Living
snippet: Urban designers and artists are turning to moss as living infrastructure. New startups use bioreceptive concrete and automated watering to help buildings filter air and stay cool during heat waves [1].
bullets: A 2026 field study in Seoul showed moss-based green roofs reduced peak roof-surface temperatures by about 19 degrees Celsius during heat waves [1].
London startup Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels made from bioreceptive concrete with controlled irrigation [1].
In Spain, leaving moss and microgreens between paving stones lowered stone surface temperatures by up to 25 degrees Celsius [1].

report.t: Cities are exploring living moss as a natural way to combat dangerous heat and regulate surface temperatures [1]. Field studies show that hydrated moss provides natural evaporative cooling for roofs and walls [1].

Startups like Alive Labs in London and Respyre in the Netherlands are creating bioreceptive concrete panels with integrated irrigation systems [1]. These systems keep moss hydrated so it can filter air, absorb noise, and lower temperatures reliably [1].
Simple observations show that leaving natural patches of moss and vegetation between paving stones can keep stone surfaces significantly cooler than bare paving [1].

why: This surprising urban innovation offers practical ways to bring calm, natural air-filtering greenery into workspaces and modern building design [1].
tryit: Explore how biophilic design or vertical greenery panels are being used in modern commercial spaces to improve indoor air quality and workspace calm [1].
qa: How does moss help cool buildings?
Hydrated moss produces natural evaporative cooling and can insulate underlying surfaces when kept moist [1].
What do startups use to grow moss on walls?
Companies use bioreceptive concrete combined with automated, integrated irrigation systems to keep the moss alive [1].
What are the environmental benefits of moss?
Moss can convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide into oxygen, act as a natural air filter, and absorb noise [1].
Why does moss need automated watering on buildings?
Dry moss exposed to direct sun can become warmer than bare mortar, so keeping it hydrated is essential for cooling [1].

title: A Rare Surviving Letter From Martha Washington Sheds Light on Epilepsy History

report.t: The Library of Congress acquired a rare letter written in Martha Washington's own handwriting for $47,500 [1]. Most of her personal correspondence was destroyed, making this document a unique historical find [1].
In the 1760 letter, Martha shared encouraging news that her young daughter Patsy was recovering from fevers and fits [1]. Historians note these symptoms were likely early signs of epilepsy [1].

Alongside the Martha Washington find, the library also acquired a letter written by Mary Todd Lincoln in 1865 [1]. These additions help researchers better understand historical figures and daily life in the past [1].

why: This historical look at early medical misunderstandings offers fascinating context on how long humans have studied neurological conditions.

title: New study shows very low regret rates for youth hormone therapy
snippet: A peer-reviewed cohort study published in JAMA Pediatrics found that regret among people who began gender-affirming hormone therapy as a minor was rare.
bullets: Only 2.7% of study participants reported some regret after starting hormone therapy as a minor [1].
The study analysed survey responses collected between 2023 and 2025 from nearly 400 participants [1].
Researchers found that 1.9% of participants felt harmed by their decision to receive hormone therapy [1].

report.t: A peer-reviewed cohort study examined satisfaction, regret and harm among people who began hormone therapy before the age of 18 [1]. Researchers analysed self-reported survey responses collected between 2023 and 2025 from a cohort of nearly 400 participants [1].

The study found that overall decisional regret was very low, with 96.8% saying it was the right decision [1]. Only 1.9% of participants said they felt harmed by their decision, and 2.7% reported some regret [1].

The authors noted the results support existing standards of care and caution against making assumptions based on demographics [1]. World Professional Association for Transgender Health board member Scott Leibowitz stated the study adds to evidence that individualised care can be beneficial [1].

why: This health research provides clear data on patient satisfaction and regret regarding gender-affirming care, which is relevant to healthcare debates in both the UK and US.
tryit: Read the full study details in JAMA Pediatrics to understand the methodology behind the survey responses collected between 2023 and 2025 [1].
qa: What percentage of participants reported regret?
Only 2.7% reported some regret, while 96.8% said it was the right decision [1].
When was the study published?
The study was published on 9 November [1].
How many participants were in the cohort?
The cohort included nearly 400 participants [1].
What did the authors say about restrictions?
They wrote that the results do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access to hormone therapy for youth [1].

sources.title: Study finds just 2.7% of youth regret hormone treatments

title: Deep sea metal nodules are actually home to diverse ocean life
snippet: New research shows that metal-rich deep-sea nodules are teeming with microscopic animals. This surprising discovery adds a new layer to debates over deep-sea mining.
bullets: Softball-size polymetallic nodules are a source of crucial metals like manganese and copper [1].
Researchers found thousands of microscopic animals living among the rock crevices of these nodules [1].
A single nodule contained an average of 17 animals and sometimes hundreds of creatures [1].

report.t: Researchers found thousands of microscopic animals living inside rock crevices of deep-sea nodules [1]. These softball-size formations sit in a desirable mining area of the Pacific Ocean [1].

Organisms collected 1,000 kilometers apart were more similar to each other than to nearby sediment communities [1]. This suggests the nodules provide a distinct habitat necessary for certain species to survive [1].
The diversity of life hiding within the nodules should factor into future plans to mine the seafloor [1]. Commercial mining could result in an irreversible loss of this unique biodiversity [1].

why: It is a fascinating scientific discovery about deep-sea ecosystems that highlights how much remains unknown about our planet's hidden biology.
tryit: Read the full Scientific Reports study online to learn more about how microscopic organisms survive in extreme deep-sea environments.
qa: What are polymetallic nodules?
They are softball-size clumps of rock and metal in the deep ocean that take millions of years to form [1].
Where were the nodules studied?
They were collected from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific Ocean [1].
What kind of creatures were found inside?
Researchers found roundworms, tiny crustaceans, and a common single-celled protist called Thurammina sp. 1 [1].
Why does this discovery matter?
It shows that commercial deep-sea mining may result in an irreversible loss of unique biodiversity associated with the nodules [1].

sources.title: These deep-sea ‘nodules’ are rich in critical minerals—and in ocean life

title: Why Genetic Editing Recreates Traits But Not Extinct Species
snippet: Recent claims about bringing back the dire wolf rely on genetic edits to grey wolf cells. Researchers argue this is lineage-genome conflation, not true de-extinction.
bullets: Biotech company Colossal Biosciences made genetic edits to grey wolf cells in order to breed animals with dire wolf characteristics in 2025 [1].
Researchers Andrew Davinack and Charlotte Daniels call this mistake lineage-genome conflation rather than true de-extinction [1].
Extinction represents the termination of an evolutionary lineage, meaning a reconstructed genome only represents a partial snapshot [1].

report.t: Biotech company Colossal Biosciences used genetic edits on grey wolf cells to create animals with larger bodies and bigger teeth in 2025 [1]. Scientists argue this is not true de-extinction [1].
Researchers call this misuse of terms lineage-genome conflation [1]. A species is an ongoing evolutionary history, not just a set of DNA sequences [1].

Using preserved cells or embryos offers a stronger claim to biological continuity, as attempted with the Pyrenean ibex back in 2003 [1]. Precise terminology helps keep technological progress in proper context [1].

why: Understanding precise technical definitions helps you evaluate emerging biotech and AI-driven biological tools with a clear, realistic lens.

They call it lineage-genome conflation [1].

Extinction represents the termination of an evolutionary lineage, and a reconstructed genome is only a partial snapshot [1].

It was published in Biology Letters [1].

title: New review reveals psychology's masculinity tests focus heavily on negative traits
snippet: A comprehensive review of 65 psychological questionnaires finds that tools measuring masculinity focus overwhelmingly on negative traits. Most instruments were tested on homogeneous groups and often fail to account for cultural background or social context.
bullets: A systematic review analyzed 65 psychological questionnaires published between 1974 and 2021 [1].
Researchers found that 78 percent of the reviewed instruments relied on a deficit-based approach focusing on negative outcomes [1].
Only 9 percent of the questionnaires provided strong evidence of external validity for broader populations [1].

report.t: Peter Fisher and his colleagues conducted a systematic scoping review of 65 quantitative masculinity scales [1]. They evaluated each tool across five dimensions including deficit focus, relational context, cultural attunement, sample diversity, and statistical quality [1].

The review found that 78 percent of the instruments relied on a deficit-based approach framing masculinity around harmful outcomes [1]. Only 22 percent incorporated strengths-based elements like responsibility or emotional openness [1].

More than half of the scales failed to account for cultural norms, and 66 percent were tested on homogeneous participant samples like white university students [1]. However, external validity and cultural attunement ratings showed improvements in scales published in the 2020s [1].

why: Understanding how standard questionnaires shape our view of human behavior helps you spot when broad surveys rely on narrow definitions.
tryit: Check out the Open Science Framework to explore pre-registered research methods and see how scientists transparently plan systematic reviews before analysing data.
qa: How many questionnaires were reviewed in the study?
The team narrowed the sample to 65 scales, consisting of 59 original questionnaires and 6 revised or shortened versions [1].
What percentage of the scales relied on a deficit-based approach?
Across the 65 reviewed instruments, 78 percent relied on a deficit-based approach [1].
Who led the systematic scoping review?
Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health in Santa Monica, California, and his colleagues conducted the review [1].
What funding did the study receive?
The work was funded by the Movember Foundation, a men’s health charity [1].

title: When Grief Changes Family Bonds: Why Distance Does Not Mean Lost Love

report.t: The death of a family member changes the relationships among everyone who remains. Family systems theory shows that when something happens to one member, the effects ripple throughout the whole family [1].

Sibling relationships move through periods of connection and disengagement. Disengagement is not always a sign of failure, but sometimes reflects a period when members need space to manage their own lives [1].
Grief is not a problem that another person can solve with quick fixes. True social support often means listening without offering advice or simply being present in the difficult emotions [1].

No, it sometimes reflects a period when family members need space to manage their own lives, emotions, or identities [1].

Cohesion and flexibility, according to the Circumplex Model of Marital and Family Systems [1].

title: Scientists Discover Exactly How Octopuses Squeeze Through Tiny Spaces
snippet: Researchers have discovered the exact step-by-step strategies octopuses use to contort their soft bodies through tiny holes. This new biological insight could help engineers improve the design of flexible search-and-rescue robots [1].
bullets: A study published November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology details how octopuses squeeze through tight gaps [1].
Common octopuses used a three-step maneuver when the hole was larger than their brain casing [1].
Engineers hope to use these findings to build soft, octopus-inspired robots for search-and-rescue missions [1].

report.t: Scientists studied common and Mayan octopuses to understand how they fit through openings ranging from about 0.4 to 1.4 inches [1]. When facing a larger hole, common octopuses probed with one arm, snaked more arms through, and used leverage to pull the rest of their body [1].

When the opening was smaller than the distance between their eyes, common octopuses divided the final step into separate stages to pull their head and mantle through [1]. Meanwhile, Mayan octopuses simply ignored smaller holes and did not try to squeeze through them [1].

Engineers want to use these insights to design flexible search-and-rescue robots that can carry sensors and tools into hard-to-reach spaces [1]. Unlike current snake-like robots, octopus-inspired machines could overcome unique environmental limitations [1].

why: It is a fascinating look at nature's problem-solving and how biological flexibility inspires practical engineering tools like search-and-rescue robots [1].
tryit: Read more about soft robotics research to see how biological discoveries are currently shaping new engineering tools [1].
qa: When was the study published?
The study was published November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology [1].
What are the only two stiffer body parts of an octopus?
They have a cartilaginous shell protecting their brains and a hard beak made of chitin [1].
What measurements were taken before the experiment?
The team measured the distance between each animal's eyes to determine the size of their brain casing [1].
How might engineers use these findings?
Engineers hope to develop flexible, octopus-like robots to navigate confined spaces during search-and-rescue missions [1].

sources.title: Octopuses Are the Ultimate Escape Artists. Now Scientists Know How the Creatures Contort Themselves to Squeeze Through Tiny Holes

title: Ancient DNA reveals surprising new timelines for Germanic and Celtic languages
snippet: New research tracking ancient DNA helps solve the enigma of how Germanic and Celtic languages spread across Europe. Scientists analysed DNA from thousands of prehistoric individuals to test specific theories on linguistic prehistory.

report.t: Researchers found that the memory of an unresolved conflict can trigger renewed emotional wounds just like the original event [1]. Ruminating on these memories without emotional control creates exponential negative effects [1].

When both partners apply integrative regulation to recalled conflicts, overall relationship satisfaction increases [1]. Acknowledging hurt feelings without generalizing them to the whole relationship helps couples move forward [1].

why: Understanding how your brain replays past arguments helps you practice self-compassion and stop small misunderstandings from derailing your peace of mind.

title: How butterfly wings could inspire safer and longer-lasting paints
snippet: Researchers are studying microscopic structures on butterfly wings to create safer paints and glitters without harmful chemical pigments.
bullets: Researchers from Northeastern University are investigating structural colour found on butterfly wings and peacock feathers [1].
Unlike standard chemical pigments that can fade or contain risky compounds, natural crystalline structures bend and scatter light [1].
The team studies crystalline pterin compounds from cabbage white butterflies to develop safe coatings with low toxicity [1].

report.t: Researchers are looking at a phenomenon called structural colour, where microscopic structures interact with light to create shimmering displays [1]. This contrasts with standard pigments like carotenoids in carrots that absorb and reflect specific wavelengths [1].

Synthetic pigments can fade in sunlight and sometimes use risky compounds containing lead, cobalt and arsenic [1]. Natural alternatives like pterin crystals found on butterfly wings offer a promising route without downstream toxicity [1].

The main challenge is to manufacture these pterin crystals at scale, as the team has only grown milligram-size crystals so far [1]. Researchers believe tweaking the size and arrangement of these crystals holds commercial potential [1].

why: This fascinating natural discovery shows how biomimicry can solve modern manufacturing problems safely.
tryit: Read more about how nature inspires sustainable design by searching for biomimicry examples online today.
qa: What is structural colour?
It is a phenomenon in which microscopic structures interact with light to create shimmering displays seen on butterflies and peacocks [1].
What are pterins?
They are crystalline compounds found on the wings of the cabbage white butterfly that can bend and scatter light [1].
What is the main challenge for researchers?
The current challenge is to manufacture pterin crystals at scale, as they have only grown milligram-size crystals so far [1].
Who is leading the research?
Leila Deravi, associate professor of chemistry and chemical biology at Northeastern University, is leading the team [1].

Bone and bronze tuning pegs discovered at the site indicate that residents played stringed instruments like lyres [1]. These instruments provided entertainment and fulfilled cultural functions around the hearth [1].

title: New study reveals that skin regenerates differently in males and females
snippet: Researchers discovered striking differences in how male and female skin stem cells renew themselves. Female skin showed a synchronized pattern that helps accelerate wound healing, while male cells acted more independently [1].
bullets: Every 6 to 7 weeks, we get an entirely new outer layer of skin due to constant cell renewal [1].
Female mouse cells showed a synchronized pattern of cell division that aids accelerated wound healing [1].
Hormones like testosterone and estrogen were shown to directly influence these differences in cell behavior [1].

report.t: An international team of researchers followed skin stem cells across five months using advanced microscopy [1]. They discovered that female skin cells renew in a synchronized, coordinated way like rowers matching their strokes [1].

When researchers manipulated hormones, they found that testosterone speeds up how fast new skin cells leave the bottom layer [1]. Removing estrogen in female mice removed most of their coordinated cell actions [1].

While this was only shown in mice so far, initial lab tests on human cells suggest the same mechanisms are at play [1]. This discovery could eventually lead to sex-tailored treatments for burns, wounds, and skin cancers [1].

why: Understanding how skin regenerates differently based on sex helps inform better approaches to personal health, skin aesthetics, and healing [1].
tryit: Ask a pharmacist or dermatologist about current evidence-based skincare routines tailored to your skin type.
qa: How often does skin renew itself?
Every 6 to 7 weeks, depending on age and body part [1].
Which institutions led the study?
Experts from the Université libre de Bruxelles in Belgium and the University of Cambridge in the UK [1].
What did testosterone do to skin cells?
Testosterone sped up the rate at which new skin cells left the bottom layer [1].
Where was the study published?
The research was published in Nature [1].

report.t: Researchers report that semaglutide repairs and restores blood vessels that power waste disposal systems in the kidneys [1]. The ingredient can now add treating chronic kidney disease to its list of health benefits [1].

A subset of 106 participants had kidney tissue samples compared before and after taking semaglutide or a placebo [1]. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes including increased blood flow, reduced scarring, and reduced blood vessel stiffness [1].

title: Surprising Study Links Animal Protein Intake To Lower Testosterone Levels

report.t: Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland examined 2,546 men aged 42 to 60 to see how protein sources affect hormone levels [1]. They found that a higher ratio of animal-to-plant protein linked to lower total testosterone [1].

Plant proteins from non-grain sources such as vegetables, legumes, or nuts were associated with higher free testosterone [1].

It means circulating testosterone was not bound to a protein in the bloodstream and was essentially up for grabs [1].
Did swapping proteins directly change levels in models?
Swapping animal protein for plant protein was not significantly associated with either total or free testosterone levels in the statistical models [1].

title: Why Larger Dogs Age Faster And What It Reveals About Mammalian Longevity
snippet: New research suggests that larger dog breeds age faster due to a loss of epigenetic control over jumping genes. Scientists hope these insights into canine aging could eventually lead to new anti-aging therapies for humans.
bullets: Researchers analyzed data from 894 dogs enrolled in the Dog Aging Project to study DNA methylation patterns across genomes [1].
Larger dog breeds lost about 35 percent more LINE1 jumping gene methylation annually than smaller breeds [1].
Scientists found that dogs with epigenetic ages older than expected showed an elevated risk of mortality [1].

report.t: While larger mammals generally live longer than small ones, the opposite happens within single species like dogs, where smaller breeds routinely outlive larger ones [1]. Large dogs grow faster, face a higher risk of age-related diseases, and die younger [1].

Researchers analyzed data from 894 dogs in the Dog Aging Project and found a broad decline in DNA methylation as dogs aged [1]. Specifically, mobile DNA sequences called LINE1s lost methylation much faster in larger breeds than in smaller ones [1].

This loss of epigenetic control over jumping genes may drive faster aging in big dogs [1]. Scientists believe targeting these transposable elements could one day help extend health spans across other mammals, including humans [1].

why: This fascinating study connects biological aging mechanics with mammalian size trade-offs, offering a peek into longevity research that may soon influence human health and health span therapies.
tryit: Read more about the ongoing findings from the Dog Aging Project online to track how shared environments and companion animal health research continue to inform human longevity studies.
qa: How many dogs were analyzed in the new study?
Researchers analyzed data from 894 dogs enrolled in the Dog Aging Project [1].
What are LINE1s?
LINE1s are mobile DNA sequences, or jumping genes, that can move around within a genome or send out copies of themselves [1].
How much faster did larger breeds lose LINE1 methylation?
Larger breeds lost about 35 percent more LINE1 methylation annually than smaller breeds did [1].

The research has been published in Science [1].

title: Why the World's Biggest Sand Sea Had No Ancient Humans

report.t: Researchers trekked approximately 1,500 kilometers across the world's largest continuous sand desert looking for signs of ancient human settlement [1]. Despite finding dozens of ancient lake beds dating back approximately 122,000 to 67,000 years ago, they found nothing made by human hands [1].

While ancient freshwater lakes provided vital hydration, the central basin's surface geology lacked suitable stone for manufacturing tools [1]. Out of 125 locations surveyed, only 10 sites on the outer margins of the desert had knappable stone [1].

The researchers developed a model showing that 57 percent of terrain accessible to water in prehistoric Arabia lacked suitable stone for tool-making [1]. This created a tethering effect where tool-dependent populations were bound to raw material sources rather than water alone [1].

why: It is a fascinating look at how ancient survival required a combination of resources rather than just a single element like water.
tryit: Read more about prehistoric archaeology or explore Open Access studies in Nature to satisfy your curiosity about ancient human migration patterns.

According to the researchers' calculations, 57 percent of the terrain lacked suitable stone for tool-making [1].

Previous research dated lake deposits in the region to approximately 122,000 to 67,000 years ago [1].

A WebKit blog post details that 40% of web page loads are from dark mode users, but only 10% of web pages natively support it [1]. Adaptive dark mode uses a color matrix to invert luminosity while preserving hue for unsupported sites [1].

Vertical tabs enable vertical navigation and drag-and-drop tab reorganization for Safari users [1]. This view makes lists easier to scan and prevents web page titles from being smushed when several tabs are open [1].

title: New psychology research challenges standard theories on how conspiracy beliefs cluster
snippet: A large-scale analysis across 17 countries challenges the idea that a broad conspiracy mentality sits at the center of people's beliefs. The findings show that general suspicion and specific claims often operate as distinct dimensions.
bullets: Psychologists often assume a broad conspiracy mentality drives specific beliefs, but new research challenges this view [1].
An analysis across 17 country samples and nearly 30,000 participants tested how general mindsets and specific claims connect [1].
Results showed that general mentality and specific conspiracy beliefs are distinct, with general mentality rarely sitting at the center of the network [1].

report.t: Researchers analyzed survey responses from nearly 30,000 participants across three comparative studies and 17 national samples to see if a general conspiracy mentality drives specific beliefs [1]. The team used network psychometrics to map how survey responses relate without assuming a single hidden cause [1].

Across the studies, general conspiracy mentality and specific claims generally formed two distinct dimensions [1]. In most of the national samples tested, the general mentality score did not act as the central hub connecting all other beliefs [1].

The contrast between different surveys suggests that results depend heavily on how questionnaires measure general mentality versus specific beliefs [1]. Because the data relied on single snapshots in time, the research cannot establish the exact direction of how these beliefs develop [1].

why: Understanding how cognitive models and belief structures work helps build self-compassion and better mental frameworks when evaluating complex information.
tryit: Review how you approach complex topics by checking if your conclusions are based on distinct evidence rather than broad assumptions.
qa: What did the new study investigate?
It tested whether a general conspiracy mentality consistently acts as the underlying cause that generates specific conspiracy beliefs [1].
How many participants were included in the analysis?
The team analyzed survey responses from nearly 30,000 participants across three comparative studies [1].
Did general mentality always sit at the center of the belief network?
No, in most of the national samples tested, the general mentality score ranked low in connection strength or was falsified as the central hub [1].
What limitation did the researchers note about the data?
Because the surveys were cross-sectional snapshots gathered at a single point in time, the research cannot establish how beliefs develop over time [1].

sources.title: New psychology research challenges a popular explanation for why conspiracy theories cluster together

title: Ecologists Document Unusually Deep Social and Sexual Bond Between Bull and Donkey
snippet: Researchers in Ethiopia observed a domesticated bull and male donkey engaging in a strong social and sexual connection. The rare study highlights complex interspecies bonds and same-sex behaviors in animals.
bullets: Ecologists observed the bull and donkey during a field research trip in Ethiopia [1].
During four days together, the bull mounted the donkey 51 times [1].
The donkey was receptive to the bull but showed aggression toward any other bull nearby [1].

report.t: Researchers in Ethiopia documented a deep social and sexual bond between a domesticated bull and a male donkey [1]. The pair, named Achille and Patroclo, were observed grazing together and engaging in numerous sexual and social interactions [1].

Scientists note that interspecies sexual interactions are rarely studied and often dismissed as random chance or mistaken identity [1]. However, the reciprocity and selectivity seen in this pair suggest a recurrent and voluntary bond [1].

Independent experts point out that because both animals are domesticated, the findings may not reflect traits common among wild populations [1]. Even so, the case study demonstrates the surprising diversity of animal social behavior [1].

why: This fascinating study expands our understanding of social relationships, diversity, and behavioral complexity in the natural world [1].
tryit: Read the full research paper in Current Biology to learn more about how ecologists study animal behavior in the field [1].
qa: What animals were involved in the study?
A domesticated bull and a male donkey living on an Ethiopian plateau [1].
How many times was the bull observed mounting the donkey?
The bull mounted the donkey 51 times over four days [1].
Who named the two animals?
The researchers named them after the ancient Greek hero Achilles and his lover Patroclus [1].
Why do experts say this case is unusual?
Most interspecies sexual interactions in literature are considered random or forced, whereas this relationship showed reciprocity and selectivity [1].

sources.title: This bull and male donkey formed an unusually deep social—and sexual—bond

title: Turn past bad food habits around with roast beetroot and sharp cheese
snippet: Transform your view of vegetables by roasting beetroot gently in its own juices. Pair this earthy sweetness with pickled raisins and sharp blue cheese for a balanced dish.
bullets: Roasting beetroot gently in its own juices concentrates its natural sweetness instead of leaching it out [1].
Pickled raisins require soaking overnight in a spiced apple cider vinegar brine [1].
Freezing the vegetarian soft blue cheese beforehand allows you to grate it finely over the finished dish [1].

report.t: Boiling vegetables can ruin their flavour and create negative associations. Roasting beetroot in sealed tinfoil parcels allows it to cook gently in its own juices and concentrate its rich earthiness [1].
Simmer apple cider vinegar with spices, garlic, herbs and chillies, then strain the liquor over golden raisins. Leave them to pickle in the fridge overnight before serving [1].
Toss the warm, peeled and quartered beetroot with the strained raisins and toasted rosemary pumpkin seeds. Finish the dish by grating frozen vegetarian blue cheese all over the top [1].

why: Changing how you cook vegetables can shift old food aversions into enjoyable, creative kitchen experiments.
tryit: Pickle a batch of golden raisins overnight using apple cider vinegar, peppercorns, allspice, bay leaves, shallots, chillies, garlic and oregano [1].

What temperature should the oven be set to for roasting the beetroot?

The vegetarian soft blue cheese should be frozen so it can be finely grated over the top [1].

They toast in the oven for 12-15 minutes [1].

snippet: Explore remarkable historical milestones, including Gary Kasparov's chess triumph, Hedy Lamarr's invention of frequency-hopping technology, and Lou Ferrigno's inspiring fitness journey.

Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil developed a frequency-hopping radio system that led to Wi-Fi and Bluetooth [1].
Lou Ferrigno began weight training at age 13 using a broomstick and pails filled with cement [1].

report.t: Gary Kasparov secured the world chess crown in Moscow by a score of 13-11, becoming the youngest champion in history [1]. Meanwhile, Hollywood star Hedy Lamarr helped design a frequency-hopping signal to prevent torpedo guidance systems from being jammed [1].

Lamarr and composer George Antheil created a system where radio signals transmitted over constantly changing frequencies [1]. This breakthrough put scientists on track to develop cellular communications, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth [1].

Fitness icon Lou Ferrigno overcame major hearing loss and bullying by turning to comic books and weight training [1]. He later underwent cochlear implant surgery at 69, bringing the star to tears of joy [1].

title: Scientists discover the first known ancient marine amphibian fossil
snippet: Researchers found that the ancient armored amphibian Gerrothorax maritimus lived in the ocean 237 million years ago, challenging long-held rules about modern amphibians.
bullets: Gerrothorax maritimus is the first amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater [1].
Chemical analysis of strontium in the fossil bones proved that the creature ate seafood and drank seawater [1].
Unlike modern amphibians, this creature retained fishy breathing gills and was covered in bony body armor [1].

report.t: Scientists found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes stalked the seafloor 237 million years ago [1]. Today, more than 8,000 amphibians are known, and none live solely in saltwater [1].

Researchers inspected two well-preserved fossils measuring around 70 centimeters found in what was once a seabed [1]. Levels of strontium in the fossil bones matched the Triassic ocean, confirming the animal lived there [1].

The creature had bony armor that prevented water loss and retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for deep life [1]. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat to unleash a suction attack on prey [1].

why: This surprising scientific discovery highlights how nature constantly defies expected rules, offering a fascinating look into prehistoric evolution.
tryit: Read the full study in Nature Ecology & Evolution to explore how ancient creatures adapted to extreme environments [1].
qa: When did Gerrothorax maritimus live?
The creature lived 237 million years ago [1].
How long was each specimen?
Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard [1].
How did scientists prove it lived in the ocean?
Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean [1].
How did the creature hunt?
Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so it could unleash a suction attack on fish and small creatures [1].

sources.title: This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

title: Geologists Rule Out Scotland as the Source of Stonehenge's Altar Stone
snippet: A new study reveals that Stonehenge's mysterious six-ton Altar Stone did not come from northeast Scotland, reopening the scientific hunt for its true birthplace.
bullets: Researchers tested 70 field samples from Scotland's Orcadian Basin but found no match for the Altar Stone [1].
A 2024 theory had previously linked the 16-foot slab to northeast Scotland, at least 465 miles away [1].
The search for the origin of the flat sandstone slab now pivots to northern England, other parts of Scotland, or Ireland [1].

report.t: Scientists previously thought a flat six-ton slab at the heart of Stonehenge came from northeast Scotland [1]. A rigorous new study has overturned that conclusion after testing 70 field samples from the region [1].

Researchers combined direct examinations with analyses of museum samples to evaluate the stone's sedimentology, geochemistry and mineralogy [1]. This created a detailed geological fingerprint used to test leading origin theories [1].

Ruling out northeast Scotland leaves the birthplace of the unique stone a mystery once again [1]. Attention now shifts to alternative formations in northern England, other parts of Scotland, or Ireland [1].

why: It is a fascinating archaeological detective story about solving ancient mysteries through modern science and persistent investigation.
tryit: Read the full study in the Journal of the Geological Society to learn how geologists build geological fingerprints for ancient rocks.
qa: Where did scientists previously think the Altar Stone came from?
They linked it to a potential source in northeast Scotland, at least 465 miles away by land [1].
How many samples were tested in the Orcadian Basin?
Researchers took about 70 samples, brought them back to laboratories and tested them [1].
Who led the new geological study?
Duncan Pirrie, an emeritus geologist at the University of South Wales, led the study [1].
Where are researchers looking now?
The search now pivots to alternative formations in northern England, other parts of Scotland or even Ireland [1].

sources.title: Where Did Stonehenge's Mysterious, Six-Ton Altar Stone Really Come From? Geologists Rule Out the Scottish Hypothesis as the Search Deepens

title: Why Americans Eat Dinner So Much Earlier Than the Rest of the World
snippet: Discover why the United States eats dinner between 5:00 and 6:00 pm, while other countries eat much later due to work schedules, sunlight, and culture [1].
bullets: Many Americans eat dinner early between 5:00 and 6:00 pm because they prioritize it as their heartiest meal after lighter breakfasts and lunches [1].
Countries like Mexico, Spain, and South American nations enjoy longer midday breaks for a filling lunch, delaying evening hunger [1].
In Spain, the sun sets as late as 9 or 10 pm, meaning daily schedules and dinner times adapt to daylight hours [1].

report.t: Americans work from 9 to 5 with a quick break for lunch, leaving little time to focus on meals until after the workday ends [1]. Other countries break up their work hours with longer midday breaks, allowing time to enjoy a big meal without rushing [1].

In France, primetime television series do not start until nearly 9 pm to ensure dinner is not rushed [1]. Countries like the U.K. and Australia plan an afternoon snack called tea time to help push their evening meal later [1].

Health and wellness TikToks cite studies saying that eating dinner early is better for digestion and sleep [1]. These studies suggest eating three hours before bedtime is best, with Gen Z influencers supporting dinner by 8 and bed by 9 [1].

why: Understanding different cultural schedules and meal structures gives you fresh insight into international work-life balances and travel timing [1].
tryit: Observe your own evening routine and test eating dinner three hours before bedtime to see how it affects your sleep and digestion [1].
qa: Why do Americans eat dinner earlier than people in other countries?
Americans often eat light breakfasts and lunches, saving their biggest meal for dinnertime and making them hungry earlier [1].
How do work schedules affect meal times in the United States?
Americans typically work from 9 to 5 with a quick lunch break, revolving their day around work rather than mealtimes [1].
Why do people in Spain eat dinner later?
The sun sets as late as 9 or 10 pm in Spain, so daily schedules adapt to keep working during daylight hours [1].
What role does social media play in American dinner times?
Health influencers on TikTok cite studies saying early dinners improve digestion and sleep, promoting trends like dinner by 8 [1].

Dead Horse State Park offers evening scorpion searches where the creatures glow a brilliant blue under UV light [1].
Sand Hollow State Park hosts monthly full-moon kayak paddles on its large reservoir from April through September [1].

report.t: Southern Utah parks are embracing night-centric recreation as millions of visitors flock to the area during scorching summer days [1]. Nighttime brings cooler temperatures, peaceful silence, and starry skies across certified dark sky parks [1].

Guided night hikes at Capitol Reef reveal ancient petroglyphs and sandstone bridges lit entirely by moonlight and stars [1]. Meanwhile, parks like Dead Horse feature evening programmes including astronomy talks and biofluorescent scorpion searches [1].

Sand Hollow State Park offers popular monthly full-moon kayak paddles allowing visitors to float on the reservoir after moonrise [1]. These evening water sessions offer a serene way to experience the landscape alongside night fishers and swimmers [1].

title: Why This Autumn Is Turning Out to Be a Bumper Year for Wild Mushrooms
snippet: A damp autumn and warm weather forecast are creating ideal conditions for wild mushrooms to pop up across the UK. Researchers recently recorded 39 different fungi species on a single woodland walk.
bullets: Researchers on a Somerset woodland walk recorded 39 different fungi and set a nationwide record for fly agaric sightings [1].
UK Met Office forecasts suggest a warm, wet autumn with chances around 1.5 times higher than normal [1].
Sightings of chicken of the woods on iNaturalist have increased by around 25% in the UK compared to last year [1].

report.t: An autumn fungi walk in Somerset revealed extensive growth, with researchers barely covering half a kilometre in an hour due to the sheer volume of specimens [1]. Findings included bright yellow stagshorn fungi and vivid purple Russulas [1].

Rainfall is one of the strongest predictors of annual mushroom productivity, acting like a balloon as water pressure expands the cells above ground [1]. Mushrooms can be up to 90% water, explaining why they pop up after rain [1].

While an abundance of certain fungi points to damp weather, high numbers of honey fungus reflect vegetation stressed by long dry summers [1]. Meanwhile, citizen science platforms like iNaturalist help experts track how species are coping [1].

why: This fascinating look at woodland ecology offers a great excuse to step outside, observe local nature, and engage with citizen science projects during a bumper season.
tryit: Head to your local woodland or grassland with a field guide or join a guided walk to spot local fungi today [1].
qa: How many species of mushrooms are there?
There are believed to be 14,000 species of mushroom and 140,000 of fungi [1].
Why do mushrooms pop up after rain?
They use water pressure within their cells to expand and push above ground, much like inflating a balloon, and can be up to 90% water [1].
What is chicken of the woods?
It is a fungus showing off cascading, bright yellow lobes bursting from urban trees, with UK iNaturalist sightings up by around 25% [1].
Can you forage wild mushrooms?
Foraging for personal use is allowed, but picking for commercial sale is illegal, and you should never eat a mushroom unless you are certain of its identity [1].

title: Decoding the fascinating slang and high-society secrets of the Gilded Age
snippet: Explore the colourful vernacular of late 19th-century New York society, from dollar princesses to the Four Hundred. Learn how historical terms evolved and discover the real meanings behind period drama slang.
bullets: In late 1800s-speak, the alum was a slangy word for the best possible outcome or situation [1].
Dollar princesses were the eligible debutante daughters of newly wealthy American industrialists married to UK aristocrats [1].
The Four Hundred was Mrs. Caroline Astor's sought-after list of the 400 most important high-society figures [1].

report.t: Late 19th-century vernacular included clever terms like the alum for a great outcome and beeswax as a name for bores [1]. These phrases added unique flavour to everyday speech during periods of rapid industrial growth [1].
Wealthy American industrialist families married their debutante daughters to cash-strapped British aristocrats [1]. This solved cash crises for the nobility while giving the brides social cachet [1].
Mrs. Caroline Astor used this famous list to separate established elite families from the nouveau riche [1]. The number supposedly matched the maximum capacity of her Fifth Avenue ballroom [1].

why: It is a fascinating linguistic look at how language and social rules evolved during periods of massive economic shifts.
tryit: Use an old-fashioned idiom or phrase in your conversation today to test how language shifts meaning over time.
qa: What does the alum mean?
It was a slangy word for the best possible outcome or situation [1].
Who were dollar princesses?
They were the eligible debutante daughters of America's newly wealthy families married off to English aristocrats [1].
What was the Four Hundred?
It was Mrs. Caroline Astor's list of the 400 most important high-society figures of the day [1].
Why was whiskey called 40 rods?

title: Air Ambulance Service Rethinks Retention Through Training and Mental Health
snippet: LifeFlight of Maine has tackled severe industry staffing shortages by raising pay equity, offering in-house mental health support, and introducing a comprehensive training academy.
bullets: In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, which is more than one every three hours [1].
The cost of training a new staff member into the organization is about $100,000 [1].
LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation, a rare move in the industry [1].

report.t: Demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled since 2015, driven by rural hospital closures and strained ground ambulance stations [1]. This year, demand has risen by another 10%, putting intense pressure on flight clinicians like nurses and paramedics [1].

Emergency medical services workers face mental health burdens with rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety, and depression over five times higher than the average American's [1]. To combat this, LifeFlight hired a full-time mental health counselor to support staff [1].

Under CEO Joe Kellner, the nonprofit launched a six- to eight-month Critical Care Academy and equalised pay between paramedics and nurses [1]. These steps helped the organisation become nearly fully staffed for the first time in nine years [1].

why: This shows how investing in staff retention, fair pay, and dedicated mental health resources can turn around high-turnover, high-stress industries.
tryit: Review your own workplace or business processes to identify where targeted training programs or peer support could reduce burnout and save onboarding costs.
qa: How many flights did LifeFlight crews fly in 2025?
LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights in 2025 [1].
What is the estimated cost to train a new worker at LifeFlight?
The cost of training a new employee into the organisation is about $100,000 [1].
How much higher are PTSD rates in EMS workers compared to the average American?
Rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety, and depression are more than five times higher than the average American's [1].
Who is the CEO of LifeFlight of Maine?
Joe Kellner became CEO in 2023 [1].

sources.title: One air ambulance service rethinks what it takes to practice medicine in the sky

title: Swiss Researchers Teach Robotic Hands to Walk Independently Like Thing
snippet: Researchers at ETH Zurich trained a standard robotic hand to walk on its fingertips, recover from falls, and operate keyboards independently. The complete setup carries its own battery and computing hardware, weighing 818 grams [1].
bullets: Researchers at ETH Zurich taught a robotic hand to walk on its fingertips, recover from falls, and press keyboard keys [1].
The team added a battery, a small computer, and a motion sensor to a commercial hand, creating an 818 gram portable unit [1].
Using reinforcement learning in simulation, the software learned to coordinate the uneven fingers into a stable walking gait [1].

report.t: Engineers developed software that lets a robotic hand walk on its fingers without needing an arm to carry it [1]. By using reinforcement learning, the system learned to shift its weight across unequal fingers and a thumb [1].

The complete setup weighs 818 grams, carrying its own power and computing hardware on its back [1]. It successfully crawled across 14 surfaces, including grass, gravel, metal grating, and wooden floors [1].

Separate controllers enabled the hand to press correct keyboard arrow keys and push a cube toward a target [1]. Future goals include combining these skills and adding onboard vision for autonomous navigation [1].

why: This breakthrough highlights how simulation and reinforcement learning can unlock advanced dexterity in compact robotic hardware, offering new automation possibilities.
tryit: Explore the arXiv preprint server to read original robotics engineering papers and study how researchers apply reinforcement learning to physical hardware.
qa: How much does the complete robotic hand setup weigh?
The complete setup weighs 818 grams, or about 1.8 pounds [1].
What surfaces was the hand tested on?
It crawled across 14 surfaces, including wooden floors, metal grating, grass, and gravel [1].
How were the robot's movements trained?
The researchers trained its control software in simulation using reinforcement learning before transferring the skills to real hardware [1].
What can the hand do besides walking?
It can right itself after a fall, press keyboard arrow keys, and push a cube toward a target [1].

sources.title: This Robotic Hand Walks on Its Fingers Like Thing From The Addams Family, And It's Creepy as Heck

title: Google Takes Over Unfinished Wyoming Data Center Project From Crusoe
snippet: Crusoe sold its unfinished Wyoming data center project to Google after construction and cost hurdles. Google now plans to invest $17 billion into developing the campus.
bullets: Crusoe confirmed it sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google [1].
Google plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus [1].
Crusoe continues to develop other major data center projects for companies like Microsoft, Oracle, and OpenAI [1].

report.t: Crusoe sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google [1]. Google took over the development after raising concerns about construction timelines and costs [1].
Google announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus [1]. Despite this setback, Crusoe recently raised a $3.9 billion funding round [1].
Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space, renting GPUs, and selling compute power for AI inference [1]. Its other projects include large campuses built for Microsoft, Oracle, and OpenAI [1].

why: It shows how major tech players navigate massive infrastructure hurdles and capital demands in the booming AI sector.
tryit: Review how infrastructure bottlenecks affect scaling timelines when planning your own technology projects or investments.

Google took over the development from Crusoe [1].

Google announced plans to invest $17 billion [1].

title: Scientists Discover a Potential Blood Biomarker for Tinnitus
snippet: Researchers have identified a blood protein called prestin that is linked to persistent ringing in the ears. This discovery offers a promising first step toward future diagnostic blood tests and treatments.
bullets: Scientists studied 82 adults, half of whom experienced tinnitus, and found a link to a blood protein named prestin [1].
Participants with tinnitus showed blood concentrations of prestin that were about 50 percent higher than those without the condition [1].
Prestin is a motor protein found in the membranes of outer hair cells in the cochlea that helps amplify sounds [1].

report.t: Scientists have found what could be the strongest evidence yet of a biomarker candidate for tinnitus in the blood [1]. The study looked at 82 adults to see how an ear protein relates to persistent ringing sounds [1].

People with tinnitus had blood concentrations of prestin that were about 50 percent higher than participants without the condition [1]. Prestin is a motor protein in outer hair cells that helps amplify sounds and is crucial for sensitive hearing [1].

While the biomarker cannot yet be used reliably for a clinical diagnosis, researchers hope this is a first step toward developing drugs to manage tinnitus [1]. Future research will help clear up how other factors might also contribute to the condition [1].

why: This research highlights how emerging scientific discoveries in blood biomarkers could soon transform subjective health complaints into measurable conditions.
tryit: Speak with a GP or a qualified health professional if you experience persistent ringing in your ears to discuss management strategies.
qa: What protein was linked to tinnitus in the study?
A protein called prestin was found to be linked to the condition [1].
How much higher were prestin levels in people with tinnitus?
Blood concentrations of prestin were about 50 percent higher in participants with tinnitus [1].
How many adults took part in the experiment?
The experiment involved 82 adults, half of whom experienced tinnitus [1].
Can prestin currently be used as a reliable diagnostic tool?
A separate diagnostic accuracy analysis suggested the biomarker cannot yet reliably be used as a tool to diagnose tinnitus [1].

sources.title: Scientists Identified a Biological Signature of Tinnitus, And It's in Your Blood

title: Why AI Spending Is Stalling Even As Token Volumes Rise
snippet: New data from Ramp shows that corporate AI spending flatlined over late summer despite rising token volumes. Intense price competition and savvier customers are creating a clear buyer's market for AI tools.
bullets: Token spend grew only 1.5% across August and September according to Ramp data [1].
OpenAI and Anthropic have both cut API prices significantly in an ongoing price war [1].
Companies are getting thriftier by using routers and budgets to route tasks to cheaper models [1].

report.t: A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose [1]. Token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September compared to a 42% jump in July [1].
The slowdown is driven by intense price cuts from major model providers and smarter customers [1]. Companies are learning to use routers and budgets to offload tasks to cheaper light models [1].
With cheap open-source models and lightweight routing tools like Jev entering the market, it has become a buyer's market [1]. Businesses can now accomplish workloads at a much lower cost [1].

why: This matters because falling API costs and intense competition mean you can build or run AI agents and business automation for a fraction of last year's budget.
tryit: Review your current software stack and test open-source models or budget-friendly routing tools to cut your monthly AI API costs.
qa: Why is AI spending stalling?
Spending is stalling due to fierce price competition, provider discounts, and companies getting better at using cheaper models [1].
How much do median firms spend on AI per employee?
Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month [1].
What is Jev?
Jev is a new lightweight tool for choosing between predetermined outputs that is increasingly among top performers on Ramp [1].
Did spending recover in October?
Yes, October data saw token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23 [1].

sources.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO | TechCrunch

title: New Report Reveals AI Accelerating Its Own Development Inside Anthropic
snippet: A new report from safety organization METR shows Anthropic using AI to speed up its own research, with models improving twice as fast as a year ago. Employees reported being around 12 times more productive when using the company's advanced internal models.
bullets: Anthropic models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores showing two years of historical progress in one year [1].
Employees using the most capable internal model reported being around 12 times as productive at their work compared to working without AI assistance [1].
Over the past six months, Anthropic finished training three unreleased models codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 [1].

report.t: Independent research organization METR published a report detailing how AI is speeding up research inside Anthropic [1]. The findings show that most of the acceleration is driven by AI itself rather than just more computing power [1].

Internal polls and interviews show staff using advanced AI models feel they are about 12 times as productive as they would be without help [1]. This increase is roughly double what employees reported a few months prior [1].

Anthropic has finished training three new unreleased models over the past six months named Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 [1]. The company heavily redacted the final public report to protect commercial interests and avoid handing out a development roadmap [1].

why: Understanding how fast frontier labs use AI to boost productivity helps you spot emerging workflow tools and business automation opportunities early.
tryit: Review your weekly workflow and identify one repetitive research or drafting task to test with a frontier AI model today.
qa: How much faster are Anthropic models improving?
They are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago [1].
What productivity gains did employees report?
Staff reported being around 12 times as productive at their work when using the most capable internal model [1].
Who published the report?
The report was published by the AI safety research organization METR following an 11-week investigation [1].
What unreleased models were identified?
METR identified three unreleased models codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4, plus an older 2022 model [1].

sources.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

title: Why companies hire externally for AI jobs despite trusting internal staff
snippet: New research shows 92% of HR leaders believe current staff can be trained for AI roles, yet half of companies still hire outside.
bullets: A study by Careerminds reveals that 92% of HR professionals believe existing employees can be reskilled for artificial intelligence roles [1].
Despite this confidence, 51% of HR professionals and 47% of managers report hiring externally for new AI positions [1].
External hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally and takes up to 20 days longer [1].

report.t: Research published by Careerminds shows a clear disconnect between belief and action in corporate AI hiring [1]. While 88% of people managers agree that internal staff can adapt, many organizations still look outward for new talent [1].

Tracking internal skills proves difficult for many companies, with 43% of HR professionals citing limited visibility as a barrier [1]. This lack of clear skill tracking stops leaders from moving current workers into new roles [1].

Response to AI workforce needs varies, with technology and telecom hiring externally 15% more often than redeploying [1]. Meanwhile, media and entertainment focuses more on internal moves, with 56% of HR pros reporting staff redeployment [1].

why: Understanding how companies approach AI staffing highlights opportunities to pitch internal automation projects or position your own AI skill set for higher-value internal roles.
tryit: Review your current workplace skills and identify one repetitive task you could automate with an AI tool this week, then pitch the efficiency gain to your manager.
qa: What percentage of HR professionals believe employees can be reskilled for AI roles?
92% of HR professionals believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles [1].
What percentage of HR professionals report that their organizations hire externally for AI positions?
51% of HR professionals report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions [1].
How many people managers and HR professionals were surveyed in the research?
The research surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers [1].
How much more expensive can external hiring be compared to internal filling?
External hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally [1].

sources.title: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs - but half of companies still hire outside - ZDNET

title: Historical Milestones from Murano Glass to the Bodleian Library
snippet: Explore fascinating historical moments on this day, including the founding of Murano glassmaking, the reopening of Oxford's Bodleian Library, and the release of Led Zeppelin's iconic fourth album.
bullets: The Republic of Venice confined its glassmaking industry to the island of Murano 735 years ago today [1].
The Bodleian Library at Oxford University reopened permanently 424 years ago today with over 13 million printed items [1].
Led Zeppelin released their fourth album 55 years ago today, which eventually shipped over 37 million copies worldwide [1].

report.t: In 1291, the Republic of Venice confined glassmaking to the island of Murano to protect trade secrets [1]. Artisans must maintain extreme physical endurance, working up to 16 hours straight to keep the glass pliable [1]. Today, the craft has evolved into fine art and sculpture, adapting successfully to modern European energy prices [1].

The Bodleian Library at Oxford University reopened permanently in 1602 under founder Sir Thomas Bodley [1]. It houses priceless treasures including J.R.R. Tolkien's manuscripts and one of the four surviving copies of the Magna Carta [1]. It stands today as the second-largest library in Britain after the British Library [1].

Recorded informally in an English country house, Led Zeppelin's fourth album was released 55 years ago [1]. Despite warnings of professional suicide for using four symbols instead of text, it rose to No.1 on the UK chart within days [1]. It became the band's best-selling record, shipping over 37 million copies worldwide [1].

why: Looking at historical milestones and creative persistence offers a refreshing perspective on long-term projects and mastery.
tryit: Visit the Bodleian Library website online to browse their digital collections and historical manuscripts.
qa: When was the death penalty abolished for almost all crimes in the UK?
The Murder Act of 1965 abolished the death penalty for almost all crimes in the UK [1].
What famous manuscripts are kept in the Bodleian Library?
The library holds many of J.R.R. Tolkien's manuscripts, a copy of the Magna Carta, and a Gutenberg Bible [1].
How many copies of Led Zeppelin's fourth album were shipped worldwide?
The album shipped over 37 million copies worldwide [1].
Who was the first African-American elected to the US Senate?
Edward Brooke was elected to the US Senate in 1966 [1].

sources.title: Good News in History, November 8 - Good News Network

title: Building Compassion and Connection Through Honest Dialogue
snippet: Farah Pandith's work shows how building compassion and listening to diverse voices can help counter extreme division and bridge gaps in communities. By exercising empathy like a muscle, people can foster understanding even amid disagreement.
bullets: Farah Pandith spent decades researching why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into us versus them [1].
She helped launch initiatives like Against Violent Extremism and Hours Against Hate to encourage meaningful dialogue [1].
More than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey for the Muhammad Ali Index [1].

report.t: Research shows that people are drawn to extremism not overnight, but when seeking recognition, certainty, or a place in the world during times of self-doubt [1]. Effective prevention relies on understanding these underlying human needs rather than just using military force [1].

Bringing former extremists into youth centers and communities creates authentic connections that official warnings cannot match [1]. Campaigns like Hours Against Hate successfully encouraged millions of teenagers to do something kind for someone different from themselves [1].

The Muhammad Ali Index on compassion measures community connection using surveys across multiple cities to help local leaders build stronger relationships [1]. Experts emphasize that compassion is a muscle that can be exercised through intentional practice [1].

why: Practicing self-compassion and recognizing your own inner state is the essential starting point for building healthier connections with others [1].
tryit: Spend one hour today doing something kind or helpful for someone whose background or perspective is different from your own [1].
qa: Who is Farah Pandith?
She is a former counterterrorism and counter-extremism expert who served under multiple U.S. presidential administrations [1].
What is the Muhammad Ali Index?
It is an initiative developing a state of compassion survey across American and global cities to help leaders build stronger connections [1].
Can compassion be trained?
Yes, Pandith and experts argue that compassion is a muscle that can be exercised through practice [1].
What campaign encouraged teenagers to help others?
The Hours Against Hate campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves [1].

sources.title: The Counter-Extremism Expert Building Our Capacity for Compassion

snippet: Studies show that laughing for 10 to 15 minutes can burn up to 40 calories. Prepping a few holiday jokes is a great way to break any awkward silence at the dinner table.
bullets: Studies show that 10 to 15 minutes of laughing can burn up to 40 calories [1].
Prepping a few jokes is the best defense against a dead-silent dinner table [1].
Jokes can help break an awkward silence before politics come up [1].

report.t: Studies show that 10 to 15 minutes of laughing can burn up to 40 calories [1]. After a large meal, you might want to double that dose [1].
Prepping a few jokes is your best defense against a dead-silent dinner table [1]. It helps break an awkward silence before politics come up [1].
Simple questions and dad jokes can give your core a workout [1]. For instance, one joke asks why the turkey passed on the pumpkin pie, with the answer being that he was stuffed [1].

title: Why the Festival of Lights Lands on Different Dates Each Year
snippet: Discover why Diwali changes its date annually. It follows a complex lunisolar calendar instead of the standard western one [1].
bullets: Diwali is known as the festival of lights and spans five days of celebrations [1].
The date changes because the Hindu calendar integrates both solar and lunar time [1].
The main day falls on Kartik Amavasya, which is a sacred day in the Hindu month of Kartik [1].

report.t: Diwali involves decorating buildings with lamps, candles, and fairy lights [1]. It is an important celebration in Hinduism, Sikhism, and Jainism [1].
The festival date changes because it follows the Hindu calendar rather than the Gregorian western calendar [1]. This calendar is known as the Panchanga and integrates both solar and lunar time [1].
The most important day of Diwali is Kartik Amavasya, the darkest day of the month [1]. This ensures the lights contrast strongly with the night sky [1].

why: Understanding different cultural calendars shows how time and language connect across different global traditions [1].
tryit: Read more about how lunisolar calendars work by checking an online cultural calendar guide today [1].
qa: What does the word Diwali originate from?
It originates from the Sanskrit word dipavali, which means a row of lights [1].
Why does the date of Diwali change?
It changes because it follows the Hindu lunisolar calendar rather than the western Gregorian calendar [1].
When does the most important day of Diwali take place?
It takes place on Kartik Amavasya, the darkest day of the month [1].
What is the Hindu calendar called?
It is known as the Panchanga [1].

sources.title: Why Is Diwali Celebrated on Different Dates Every Year?

title: OpenAI introduces a new GIF generator feature in ChatGPT
snippet: OpenAI has launched a new moving images feature for ChatGPT that lets you turn text prompts or photos into animated GIFs. While complex movements still look strange, it is a fun tool for making lighthearted memes.
bullets: OpenAI introduced a new GIF support feature in ChatGPT as an animation tool [1].
You can generate a GIF by giving ChatGPT a detailed prompt or by using your own sketches and images as a base [1].
You can edit the results by asking ChatGPT to make the GIF longer, shorter, or change the style [1].

report.t: OpenAI has launched GIF support for ChatGPT as its first moving images feature since Sora was shut down [1]. The tool allows users to turn text prompts or still images into animated GIFs within seconds [1].

Users can refine their creations by asking ChatGPT to make adjustments such as slowing down transitions, removing objects, or altering the style [1]. The feature works well for simple loops and festive graphics, though complex movements can look unnatural [1].

While the tool is fun for casual memes, traditional human-made GIFs from real video clips remain the gold standard for capturing intricate details like steam and bubbles [1]. ChatGPT excels when used for lighthearted, fun animations rather than hyper-realistic physical processes [1].

why: It is a fun and creative tool to test out when you want to make quick, custom graphics or memes to share in group chats.
tryit: Open ChatGPT, write a detailed prompt for a simple loop or upload one of your own sketches, and use follow-up commands to edit the resulting animation.
qa: What is the new feature in ChatGPT?
OpenAI added GIF support, allowing users to generate animated GIFs from text prompts, sketches, or still images [1].
Can you edit the generated GIFs?
Yes, you can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove objects, change the style, or slow down transitions [1].
What does ChatGPT do best with this feature?
It excels at making fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes where you do not look too closely at complex physical details [1].
What are the limitations of the tool?
Complex movements and transitions are not fully nailed down, leading to weird hand shifts and objects appearing unexpectedly [1].

sources.title: ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

title: Tracing The Real Locations Of A New Chile Film
snippet: Follow the trail of a new film from the streets of Santiago to the moai statues of Rapa Nui. Explore historical sites and filming locations across Chile.
bullets: Abercrombie and Kent launched a 9-day itinerary to follow the trail of the film Wild Horse Nine [1].
Travelers can visit La Moneda Palace and the Salvador Allende Museum of Solidarity in Santiago [1].
On Rapa Nui, visitors can see iconic sites like the moai statues at Ahu Akivi and the Iorana Hotel [1].

report.t: The journey starts in Santiago, where visitors can view the historic La Moneda Palace and explore the Salvador Allende Museum of Solidarity [1]. These locations offer deep context into the country's turbulent 1970s history [1].
Flights bring travelers to Rapa Nui, where local guides lead tours past volcanic stone moai statues and wild horses [1]. Visitors can also view the preserved set at the retro Iorana Hotel [1].

Film-inspired travel is growing in popularity, prompting new tour offerings that connect cinema with real-world history and geography [1]. This route lets travelers experience the landscapes seen on screen firsthand [1].

why: This offers a practical blueprint for combining cultural exploration with modern screen tourism on your next trip.

The characters travel from their station in Santiago to the Polynesian island of Rapa Nui [1].

Tour operator Abercrombie and Kent launched a 9-day itinerary to chase the film's trail [1].
