title: Go first: the opening number quietly wins the deal
snippet: In three experiments, whoever made the first offer got the better outcome, and that number predicted the final price.
bullets: Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001): across 3 experiments, the side that made the first offer, buyer or seller, did better.[1]
First offers were a strong predictor of the final settlement price.[1]
The edge vanished when the other side focused on its own target or the opponent's alternatives.[1]

report.t: An opening number drags the whole conversation toward it. That's the anchoring effect, and negotiation is one of its best-studied arenas.[2] Negotiators who set the first offer often get better economic results.[2]
The anchor lost its power when the receiver thought about their own target, the other side's walk-away price, or the other side's alternatives.[1] It worked face to face and by email.[1]
Open first when you know the market well. When they open first, don't argue with their number. Pull your attention back to your own target and alternatives.[1]

1. Research the realistic range. 2. Open first with a confident, well-reasoned number near the ambitious end. 3. If they open first, pause and restate your own target before responding. The research shows the first offer strongly predicts the final price.[1]

why: When you sell a car, price a service or buy a business, your first number is a lever, not a guess.
tryit: Before your next deal, write down your target and walk-away price. If they anchor first, reread your note before you reply.
qa: Should I always make the first offer?
The studies found first-movers did better, but the advantage disappeared if the other side focused on its own target or alternatives.[1] It works best when you know the value well.
How do I resist someone else's anchor?
Shift focus to your own target, their reservation price or their alternatives. In the experiments, that cancelled the first-offer advantage.[1]
Does it work over email?
Yes. The effects showed up in face-to-face and email negotiations.[1]
What is the anchoring effect?
A bias where an initial number strongly influences later judgements. It shows up in negotiation and pricing.[2]

title: Your secret weapon in any negotiation is your walk-away plan
snippet: BATNA, the Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement, came out of Harvard's Program on Negotiation. It decides who can say no.
bullets: BATNA was developed by Roger Fisher and William Ury of Harvard's Program on Negotiation.[1]
It first appeared in their principled-negotiation books starting with Getting to YES (1981).[1]
Harvard PON advises translating your BATNA into the terms of the current deal.[2]

report.t: Your BATNA is what you'll do if this deal dies. The better it is, the calmer and firmer you can be.[1]
Fisher and Ury introduced it in Getting to YES in 1981, as part of 'principled negotiation'.[1]
Harvard's PON suggests converting your alternative into the same terms as the deal on the table, so you compare like with like.[2]

report.h: Build it before you need it
report.t: Most people think about alternatives only when talks stall. Do it first: list your options, pick the best one, and price it. Harvard PON stresses translating it into the deal's terms.[2] Then you'll know exactly when a 'no' is better than a bad 'yes'.

why: Buying or selling a UK business, or asking for a better rate, goes better when you've built a real Plan B first.
tryit: Pick one upcoming negotiation. Write your BATNA in one sentence and put a £ number on it.
qa: What does BATNA stand for?
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you'll do if no deal is reached.[1]
Who invented it?
Roger Fisher and William Ury of Harvard's Program on Negotiation, in Getting to YES (1981).[1]
How do I improve my BATNA?
Develop real alternatives before you negotiate, then translate them into the deal's terms so you know when to walk.[2]
Is BATNA the same as my bottom line?
Not quite. The BATNA is the alternative itself; your walk-away point comes from comparing it with the deal.[2]

title: Name the feeling and it shrinks, in you and across the table
snippet: Putting feelings into words ('affect labeling') measurably calms the brain's alarm system. Skilled negotiators use it on purpose.
bullets: Affect labeling means putting feelings into words.[1]
Studies link it to less distress, reduced amygdala activity and lower skin-conductance response.[1]
It's a relatively new emotion-regulation technique, often confused with reappraisal.[1]

report.t: Saying 'I feel anxious' sounds too simple to work. Yet labeling has been linked to reduced amygdala activity and lower physical stress responses.[1]
Labeling isn't reframing. You don't change the story, you just name what's there.[1]
In tense talks, a calm 'It sounds like timing is the real worry' gives the other person a name for their feeling. That's a practical extension, not a lab finding.

For you: 'I'm noticing frustration.' For them: 'It sounds like the timeline is stressful.' Then stop talking. Research links labeling emotions to less distress and a calmer amygdala response.[1] Silence after a label gives the other person room to open up.

why: Calmer you, clearer deals. And people trust negotiators who make them feel understood.
tryit: Next tense moment, silently name your own feeling in 3 words. Then try one 'It sounds like…' out loud.
qa: What is affect labeling?
Putting feelings into words, which research links to reduced emotional reactivity.[1]
Does it really change the brain?
Studies have measured reduced amygdala activity and lower skin conductance when people label emotions.[1]
Is it the same as positive thinking?
No. It's often confused with reappraisal, but labeling just names the feeling without changing its meaning.[1]
How do I use it in a negotiation?
Name the emotion you notice ('It seems this feels rushed'), then pause. The lab evidence is about labeling your own feelings; using it on others is a practical extension.

sources.title: Affect labeling

title: A small, unasked-for favour makes people want to say yes
snippet: In a classic 1971 experiment, people bought more raffle tickets from someone who'd given them a free drink, whether or not they liked him.
bullets: Dennis Regan's 1971 study tested how a favour and liking affect compliance.[1]
People felt indebted even after an uninvited favour.[1]
That held irrespective of whether they liked the person who did the favour.[1]

report.t: Participants thought they were rating art with a partner, 'Joe', who was secretly part of the study. Sometimes Joe brought them a drink, unasked.[1]
People felt indebted even from uninvited favours, and liking didn't decide it.[1]
In sales and deals, leading with real value, such as an intro or a useful insight, taps a deep social rule. Keep it honest; manipulation backfires.

A useful article, a warm introduction, a quick tip about their market, or simply your full attention. Regan found people felt indebted even when the favour wasn't requested.[1] Give without strings, and later ask clearly and fairly.

why: Before you ask for a meeting, a discount or a referral, give something useful first.
tryit: Today, send one person something genuinely helpful with no ask attached.
qa: What did Regan find?
A small favour increased compliance with a later request, even when the favour was uninvited.[1]
Does it matter if they like me?
In the study, the sense of indebtedness held irrespective of liking.[1]
How do I use this ethically?
Give real value first and make the later ask fair. The research describes the social rule; how you use it is your choice.
What is reciprocity in psychology?
The social norm of responding to a positive action with another positive action.[1]

sources.title: Reciprocity (social psychology)

title: £20,000 a year the taxman can't touch
snippet: In 2026-27 you can put up to £20,000 into ISAs, and the interest and gains stay tax-free.

Interest in ISAs usually isn't taxed, unlike ordinary savings accounts.[2]

Cash, stocks and shares, innovative finance and Lifetime ISAs.[1] You must be 18 or over to open one.[1]

£20,000 in the 2026-27 tax year, across all your ISAs.[1]

Cash, stocks and shares, innovative finance and Lifetime ISAs.[1]

You must be 18 or over; gov.uk lists the full rules.[1]

10% up to 5 April 2025, then 14%, and now 18% on disposals from 6 April 2026.[1]
Timing, structure and eligibility all move the after-tax number. That's why serious buyers and sellers bring in a tax adviser early.

Do I qualify for BADR? Which tax year will the sale fall in? How does the rate change affect my net proceeds? The rate rose to 18% for disposals from 6 April 2026.[1] Getting these answers early can shape how you negotiate price and timing.

title: Before you buy a business, investigate like a detective
snippet: Due diligence is how buyers check a company before a merger or acquisition. It can also protect you legally.
bullets: A classic example: a buyer evaluates a target company before a merger or acquisition.[1]
Done well, it improves the amount and quality of information behind the decision.[1]
It may also offer a defence against legal action.[1]

report.t: Due diligence means checking a company and its assets before you commit.[1]
The point is decision quality: more and better information before you sign.[1] What you find often feeds into price talks.

report.t: The British Business Bank, the UK's government-owned economic development bank, has resources for small businesses.[2]

Customer concentration, unexplained cash swings, key contracts that end soon, staff disputes and unpaid tax. Finding these before signing gives you better information and leverage on price.[1] The British Business Bank offers guidance for small-business owners.[2]

Hyperfocus is intense concentration on one subject or task.[2] The trick is choosing what gets it before it chooses for you.

Pick one high-value task. Remove other tabs. Put water and a snack nearby. Set an alarm for 90 minutes as a stop cue. Hyperfocus is intense absorption in one task,[2] and the study shows it's a real, common ADHD experience,[1] so plan for it.

title: The 'if-then' trick that turns intentions into action

Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 meta-analysis pulled together the evidence on if-then plans and goal achievement.[1]
Tying an action to a cue means you don't have to rely on remembering it.

An if-then plan that links a situation to a goal-directed action.[1]

report.t: Self-kindness means being warm with yourself when you hit pain or shortcomings, instead of harsh.[1]

Mindfulness means seeing the pain clearly without blowing it up.[1] Neff's free exercises make it practical.[2]

Self-kindness, common humanity and mindfulness, as defined by Kristin Neff.[1]

report.t: A digital permission to travel to the UK, Jersey, Guernsey or the Isle of Man for up to 6 months.[1]
Most visitors need an ETA or a visa, depending on nationality. Europeans usually need an ETA.[1]
An ETA doesn't guarantee entry, and imitation sites charge extra.[1]

Send friends and family the official gov.uk link and remind them to apply before booking non-refundable travel. The ETA costs £20 and copycat sites charge more.[1] It lets them visit for up to 6 months, but doesn't guarantee entry.[1]

why: Friends or family visiting you from Europe need to sort this before they fly.
tryit: Send visiting friends the official gov.uk ETA link, not a search ad.
qa: How much does a UK ETA cost?
How long can I stay?
Up to 6 months.[1]
Do Europeans need one?
Usually, yes, rather than a visa.[1]
Does it guarantee entry?
Who needs an ETA?
Most visitors need an ETA or a visa, depending on nationality; gov.uk has a checker.[1]

title: The US ESTA fee nearly doubled to $40
snippet: Since 30 September 2025, the ESTA for visa-waiver visitors to the US costs $40, up from $21.
bullets: The ESTA fee rose from $21 to $40 on 30 September 2025.[1]
$10 processing for everyone, plus $30 if approved.[2]
If you're refused, you pay only the $10.[2]

report.t: A new US law raised the ESTA fee to $40 from 30 September 2025.[1]
$10 processing, then $30 on approval: a $17 travel promotion fee plus a $13 general fund fee.[2]
Third-party sites charge more, and CBP can't refund them. Use the official site only.[2]

Check if your current ESTA is still valid before applying again. Only use the official CBP site, because third-party sites charge extra and CBP can't refund them.[2] The official fee is $40, split into processing and authorisation.[2]

why: One official click saves money and hassle on every US trip.
tryit: Check your ESTA expiry date on the official CBP site before you book flights.
qa: How much is ESTA now?
$40 since 30 September 2025.[1]
What if I'm refused?
You pay only the $10 processing fee.[2]
Why was I charged more?
You may have used a third-party site. CBP can't refund those fees.[2]
Why did it go up?
Congress added a Treasury General Fund fee and raised the operational fee.[2]

title: Europe now takes your fingerprints at the border
snippet: The EU Entry/Exit System replaced passport stamps for UK and other non-EU travellers. It's been fully live since April 2026.
bullets: EES launched on 12 October 2025 and became fully operational on 10 April 2026.[1]
UK passport holders give fingerprints and a photo on their first visit. It's free.[2]
It applies to non-EU nationals on short stays. Ireland and Cyprus aren't covered.[1][2]

report.t: EES records entries and exits digitally instead of stamping passports.[1]
Expect fingerprints and a face photo on your first entry, and possibly a longer wait.[2]
EES is for non-EU nationals.[1] If you hold an EU passport, you're outside it, so carry the right one.

Arrive with extra time on your first post-EES trip, since registration can take longer.[2] EES applies to non-EU nationals.[1] If you're also an EU citizen, show your EU passport in Schengen. Through Dover, Folkestone or St Pancras, checks happen before you leave the UK.[2]

why: If you have an EU passport, using it in Schengen keeps you out of EES entirely.
tryit: Before your next EU trip, decide which passport you'll use and keep it with your boarding pass.
qa: What is EES?
The EU's digital Entry/Exit System, which registers non-EU travellers with fingerprints and a photo.[1]
When did it start?
12 October 2025, fully operational from 10 April 2026.[1]
Do I pay for EES?
No, registration is free.[2]
Does it apply to Ireland or Cyprus?
Do EU citizens need it?
No. It applies to non-EU nationals.[1]

title: ETIAS is coming: €20 for 30 European countries
snippet: The EU's travel authorisation for visa-exempt visitors isn't live yet. When it is, it'll cost €20.
bullets: ETIAS will cover visa-exempt travellers to 30 European countries.[1]
It's not running yet. The EU says it will announce the start date several months ahead.[1]
The fee is EUR 20, and stays are up to 90 days.[1]

report.t: An online permission before travel, similar to the US ESTA, for 30 European countries.[1]
No applications are being taken. The EU says it'll give several months' notice.[1]
EES is the free fingerprint check at the border. ETIAS is a separate paid online permission.[2]

Nothing to pay yet. Any site charging for ETIAS today isn't official, as the system isn't running.[1] When it launches, the official fee will be EUR 20 for visa-exempt travellers.[1] EES, the free biometric border check, is already live.[2]

why: Don't pay any website for ETIAS today. It isn't open yet.
tryit: Bookmark the official EU ETIAS page so you're ready when the launch date is announced.
qa: How much will ETIAS cost?
Is it live?
No. It isn't running yet.[1]
How long can I stay?
Up to 90 days.[1]
Is ETIAS the same as EES?
No. EES is the free border biometric record; ETIAS is a separate paid authorisation.[2]

title: The UK scrapped non-dom status. Here's the new 4-year rule
snippet: Since 6 April 2025, UK tax depends on residence, not domicile. New arrivals can get a 4-year break on foreign income.
bullets: The remittance basis ended on 6 April 2025.[1]
Qualifying new residents (after 10 years abroad) can claim relief on foreign income and gains for 4 years.[1]
Claiming means losing your tax-free personal allowance and CGT allowance.[1]

report.h: Domicile is out, residence is in
report.t: UK tax now hinges on tax residence under the Statutory Residence Test, not domicile.[2]
If you become UK resident after 10 years of non-residence, you can claim relief on eligible foreign income and gains for up to 4 tax years.[1]
Claiming costs your personal allowance and CGT annual exemption, and you claim on your Self Assessment return.[1]

report.h: Questions to ask a tax adviser
report.t: Am I UK tax resident under the Statutory Residence Test? Do I qualify for the 4-year FIG regime? Is claiming worth losing my personal allowance?[1] Residence-based rules replaced domicile from 6 April 2025,[2] so old non-dom advice may be out of date.

why: With several nationalities, your UK tax depends on where you're resident, not which passports you hold.
tryit: If you have income abroad (Brazil, EU), book one session with a cross-border tax adviser.
qa: What replaced non-dom?
A residence-based system, with a 4-year FIG regime for qualifying new residents, from 6 April 2025.[1]
Who qualifies?
UK tax residents in their first 4 years after at least 10 years of non-UK residence.[1]
What's the catch?
You lose tax-free allowances for Income Tax and CGT when you claim.[1]
How do I claim?
On your Self Assessment tax return.[1]
Is this tax advice?
No. It's general gov.uk information.

title: Brazilian and British? Both countries are fine with that
snippet: The UK allows dual citizenship, and since October 2023 Brazil places no restriction on dual nationality.
bullets: Dual citizenship is allowed in the UK, and you don't need to apply for it.[1]
Since October 2023, Brazil doesn't restrict dual nationality.[2]
Since May 2016, Brazil doesn't make naturalised citizens give up their old nationality.[2]

report.t: You can be a British citizen and a citizen of other countries, with no application needed.[1]
Brazil removed restrictions on dual nationality in October 2023.[2]
More passports can mean more options, like entering Schengen on an EU passport, which keeps you outside EES.[3]

Keep all passports valid; renewals can take months. Use the right passport at each border. In Schengen, an EU passport keeps you outside EES.[3] The UK doesn't require you to apply for dual citizenship,[1] and Brazil has no restriction since October 2023.[2]

why: Your multiple nationalities are an asset. Know the rules and use them.
tryit: Check the expiry dates on all your passports today and set renewal reminders 9 months ahead.
qa: Does the UK allow dual citizenship?
Yes, and you don't need to apply for it.[1]
Can Brazilians hold another nationality?
Yes. Since October 2023 Brazil imposes no restriction on dual nationality.[2]
Can Brazil take away my citizenship?
Only in narrow cases for naturalised citizens, such as fraud.[2]
Which passport should I use in Europe?
EES applies to non-EU nationals, so an EU passport keeps you outside it.[3]

title: Your accent isn't the problem. Clarity is
snippet: In a classic study, how strong an accent was didn't slow listeners down. Hard-to-understand speech did.
bullets: Munro & Derwing (1995): 20 native listeners judged true/false sentences from native and accented speakers.[1]
Speech rated hard to understand took longer to process.[1]
But the strength of the accent wasn't linked to processing time.[1]

report.t: Listeners weren't slowed down by how strong the accent was.[1]
What slowed listeners was speech rated hard to understand.[1]
Work on the sounds and stress that cause misunderstandings, not on erasing where you're from.

Focus on what blocks understanding: word stress (PHOtograph vs phoTOgraphy), clear vowel length, and pausing between ideas. The study found accent strength itself didn't slow listeners; low comprehensibility did.[1] Record yourself and ask: would a busy listener catch every word?

why: Your Brazilian accent is part of you. Clarity is what changes how you're heard.
tryit: Record a 30-second voice note, play it back, and mark one word a listener could mishear. Practise just that word.
qa: Does a foreign accent make me harder to understand?
Not by itself. Accent strength wasn't related to processing time; comprehensibility was.[1]
What should I focus on?
Being easy to understand: the sounds and stress patterns that cause misunderstandings.[1]
Who did this study?
Murray Munro and Tracey Derwing, in Language and Speech, 1995.[1]
Was it Portuguese speakers?
No. The accented speakers were native Mandarin speakers.[1]

sources.title: Processing time, accent, and comprehensibility in the perception of native and foreign-accented speech

title: Shadowing: repeat native speech a split second behind
snippet: Speech shadowing, repeating what you hear with a tiny delay, is a lab technique that's also used for language learning.
bullets: Speech shadowing means repeating speech with a short delay after you hear it.[1]
The delay reflects how long the brain takes to process and respond.[1]
It's used in language learning, interpreting and singing.[1]

report.t: Play audio and speak along a beat behind, copying the rhythm and melody.[1]
It trains listening and speaking at once, which is why it's used in language learning and interpreting.[1]
No textbook needed. Just a podcast you love and 5 minutes.

1. Listen to a 30-second clip once. 2. Play it again and speak along a beat behind. 3. Repeat three times, then record yourself. Shadowing is a recognised technique in language learning and interpreting.[1] Pick speakers whose style you'd like to sound like.

why: It builds the music of English, its rhythm and stress, which shapes how natural you sound.
tryit: Pick a 1-minute clip from a podcast you like and shadow it 3 times today.
qa: What is shadowing?
Repeating speech with a short delay after hearing it.[1]
Is it used for language learning?
Yes, along with interpreting and singing.[1]
How long should I practise?
Start with 5 minutes a day so it's easy to stick with.
What should I shadow?
Clear speech you enjoy, like a favourite podcast host.

sources.title: Speech shadowing

title: Learn words right before you forget them
snippet: Spaced repetition brings words back at growing intervals. It's ideal for vocabulary.
bullets: Spaced repetition schedules reviews at growing intervals to beat the forgetting curve.[1]
It's especially well suited to learning vocabulary.[1]
Anki has used the FSRS scheduler since version 23.10.[1]

report.t: Review just as a memory starts to fade, and each review lasts longer.[1]
It shines when you need to learn lots of items and keep them for good.[1]

report.h: Let the app do the timing
report.t: Apps like Anki schedule your reviews automatically.[1]

Put the phrase in a real sentence, add the audio if you can, and keep each card to one idea. Spaced repetition is especially well suited to vocabulary.[1] Apps like Anki schedule reviews just as you're about to forget.[1] Five minutes a day is plenty.

why: Phrasal verbs and idioms stick when an app brings them back at the right moment.
tryit: Add 5 English phrases you heard this week to a spaced-repetition app.
qa: What is spaced repetition?
Reviewing material at increasing intervals to beat the forgetting curve.[1]
Is it good for vocabulary?
Yes, it's well suited to vocabulary.[1]
Which app?
Anki is a popular option and uses the FSRS scheduler.[1]
How many words a day?
Start small, 5 to 10 new items, so reviews stay manageable.
